highlights: Strategic balancing between Europe and Russia

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies while pressing Algiers on migration and regional security. Algeria retains substantial bargaining power, but hydrocarbon concentration limits long-term autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel competition
frictionVectors.details: Algeria’s rivalry with Morocco and concern over instability in the Sahel constrain regional economic integration. External security partnerships near its borders increase pressure on its non-alignment posture.

highlights: Oil revenues still anchor state power

frictionVectors.title: Oil and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies and lenders retain major influence over production, while debt-service obligations reduce the state’s effective control of export revenues. Falling or volatile oil prices would quickly tighten fiscal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US, European, and Gulf interest because of its route to critical-mineral zones. The investment can improve infrastructure, but competing outside interests may limit Angola’s leverage over strategic logistics.

highlights: Cotton and logistics remain strategically exposed

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and trade disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger and regional sanctions have disrupted traditional trade routes and raised security costs around northern Benin. This threatens the autonomy of port revenues and agricultural supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and regional financing supports roads, port expansion, and energy projects. These links are economically useful but leave critical infrastructure vulnerable to creditor, security, and geopolitical bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is seeking a larger share of diamond value and greater domestic beneficiation as the long-standing De Beers relationship evolves. The government has leverage, but the narrow export base makes prolonged commercial friction costly.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are exploring Botswana’s copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects. Diversification could strengthen sovereignty, provided licensing and processing arrangements prevent a new dependence on raw-material exports.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are increasing state participation, revising mining rules, and challenging foreign operators to capture more gold revenue. This strengthens formal sovereignty but risks reduced investment, production disruptions, and expanded informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russia is intended to replace Western support, but opaque arrangements and heightened militia activity create uncertainty over access, payments, and strategic concessions. Persistent insurgency limits the state’s practical control over mining zones and transport corridors.

highlights: Mining ambitions constrained by weak governance

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals licensing
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-earth activity remains vulnerable to opaque licensing, informal production, and external trading networks. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture value or enforce environmental standards.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border and aid pressure
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda and insecurity linked to eastern DRC complicate cross-border trade and security cooperation. Dependence on external aid narrows Bujumbura's policy room.

frictionVectors.title: Port and airport external dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in ports, airports, and digital infrastructure strengthens connectivity but can create strategic dependence over critical assets. Praia is balancing European, Chinese, and broader Atlantic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing and maritime surveillance
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's extensive maritime zone is difficult to monitor, exposing fisheries to illegal, unreported, and unregulated activity. Limited patrol capacity constrains sovereign control over blue-economy resources.

highlights: Oil and infrastructure sovereignty under strain

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, dams, and industrial projects expand connectivity but increase exposure to repayment, procurement, and strategic-dependence risks. Cameroon retains formal control while negotiating from a position of fiscal constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea and anglophone insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest regions undermines local resource governance and transport corridors. Offshore oil, gas, and maritime routes also remain vulnerable to smuggling and regional security shocks.

highlights: Security sovereignty tied to Russian support
Gold and diamonds remain externally captured

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime survival while reducing strategic autonomy and increasing political leverage for Moscow-linked actors. Security cooperation also shapes access to mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond extraction is dominated by informal networks and poorly monitored concessions involving foreign operators. Weak enforcement limits state revenue and heightens conflict around mineral corridors.

highlights: Sahel and Sudan crises reshape alignments

frictionVectors.title: Oil pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's export model depends heavily on the pipeline through Cameroon and foreign energy operators, leaving revenue and logistics vulnerable to external bargaining. Fiscal dependence on oil limits diversification and strengthens executive control.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and foreign security ties
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan creates refugee, arms-trafficking, and border-security pressures in eastern Chad. N'Djamena is balancing relations with Western partners, Gulf states, and emerging Russian-linked networks while seeking to preserve regime autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: France and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute remains the central sovereignty issue, constraining relations with France while Comoros seeks diplomatic and economic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy projects rely heavily on foreign donors and partners, limiting domestic control over long-term development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral supply-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains exposed to foreign firms, opaque intermediaries, and weak state oversight, limiting the country's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern border conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and regional actors threatens mining corridors and national sovereignty while increasing dependence on external security and diplomatic intervention.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances remain heavily tied to oil exports, leaving fiscal sovereignty vulnerable to price shocks and the bargaining power of international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and energy projects expand connectivity but can constrain policy flexibility through debt, repayment, and contractor dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of export chains
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa, minerals, energy, and logistics remain closely tied to multinational capital, although processing policies are gradually increasing domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern infrastructure and border resources, encouraging reliance on external security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-base competition
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of foreign military facilities gives Djibouti leverage but also embeds its sovereignty in competition among the United States, China, France, Japan, and other partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major port and corridor infrastructure is central to national revenue yet remains exposed to foreign ownership, debt obligations, and regional trade disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's dam operations remain a strategic threat to Egypt's long-term water security. Cairo is intensifying diplomatic and security partnerships to preserve its Nile position.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Gulf Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large external financing needs give the IMF and Gulf investors influence over state assets, currency policy, and strategic infrastructure. Suez Canal revenues remain sovereign-controlled but vulnerable to regional shipping disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining production is increasing reliance on foreign technical partners and forcing the government to seek new offshore investment. Falling hydrocarbon income constrains sovereign spending and diversification.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders remain central to offshore production, LNG processing, and export logistics. Malabo retains formal control but has limited leverage over the capital and technology needed to sustain the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects provide hard currency but depend on foreign operators and capital. The government maintains tight political control while remaining exposed to disputes over labor, contracts, and revenue sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf states, Iran-linked networks, and Western naval forces raises the strategic value of Eritrean ports. External security interest could increase investment but also narrow Asmara's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African markets, transport corridors, electricity links, and customs revenue. This provides stability but limits independent control over supply chains and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Agribusiness Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and commercial agriculture remain exposed to external buyers, climate variability, and regional water constraints. Foreign ownership and export concentration limit the gains from nominal domestic resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Addis Ababa's control over its hydropower resources but continues to provoke Egyptian and Sudanese objections. Water diplomacy remains vulnerable to broader regional conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and infrastructure financing leave Ethiopia negotiating from a constrained position with China, Gulf states, and Western lenders. Telecom liberalization and port-access deals may attract capital while reducing exclusive state control over strategic networks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign concession renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition government is seeking greater Gabonese control and local processing in manganese, oil, and timber. Renegotiating terms with established foreign operators could strain investment and diplomatic ties.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export capacity remains tied to the Transgabon railway and Owendo port, requiring external capital and technical expertise. Infrastructure delays could limit the state's ability to convert resource wealth into fiscal strength.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries access and enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure and limited monitoring weaken control over coastal resources. Licensing revenue remains important, but enforcement capacity is insufficient to prevent depletion and illegal activity.

frictionVectors.title: Border and transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for surrounding trade routes, transport links, and regional market access. This dependence is practical but constrains independent infrastructure and customs policy.

frictionVectors.title: External mining control
frictionVectors.details: Gold, bauxite, and emerging lithium projects remain dominated by foreign capital and technical operators. Accra is pressing for stronger local participation and value addition while managing investor concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and policy conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-supported reforms and debt restructuring narrow fiscal room for independent industrial policy. Debt service pressures can encourage rapid resource monetization and reduce bargaining leverage with external financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project depends on multinational consortia, large-scale rail construction, and a dedicated port. Guinea may gain unprecedented export power, but foreign operators retain substantial control over financing, logistics, and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite social and environmental pressure
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain central to state revenue while generating land, water, and community grievances. Competition among Chinese, Russian-linked, and other foreign interests complicates Conakry's effort to impose consistent national standards.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fisheries access
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime surveillance leaves coastal fisheries vulnerable to overfishing and opaque licensing arrangements. External fleets capture much of the value while domestic enforcement and processing remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Port and illicit-economy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on external infrastructure and persistent cocaine-trafficking networks erode state control over maritime gateways. Political instability increases the risk that foreign commercial or security actors can influence strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese infrastructure obligations constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Debt servicing pressures continue to shape decisions on ports, railways, and public assets.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and Lamu remain focal points for Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional commercial influence. Kenya is seeking diversified partnerships while resisting arrangements that could compromise strategic infrastructure control.

highlights: Water Sovereignty Tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: HIGHLANDS WATER DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa generate vital revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on Pretoria for project financing, access, and security. Expansion of the Highlands Water Project may deepen this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: SOUTH AFRICAN ECONOMIC DOMINANCE
frictionVectors.details: South African firms, supply chains, and labor markets remain central to Lesotho's economy. This limits Maseru's bargaining power over infrastructure, customs, and industrial policy.

highlights: Iron Ore Revival, Limited Local Capture

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign operators and external capital. Liberia is seeking better royalties, jobs, and local processing while facing strong pressure to approve rapid expansion.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and mineral-export corridors attract competing Western, Chinese, and regional interests. Weak domestic infrastructure increases Liberia's dependence on outside firms for transport and export capacity.

highlights: Oil Wealth Split Between Rival Authorities

frictionVectors.title: OIL GOVERNANCE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, terminals, and revenue flows. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, armed bargaining, and competing claims to state legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY SPONSORSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and European actors retain influence through security ties, energy interests, or migration cooperation. Their involvement limits Libya's autonomous control over strategic infrastructure and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, graphite, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export networks. Madagascar is attempting to increase domestic value capture but remains exposed to investor pressure and commodity-price swings.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND ENERGY BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Limited electricity, roads, and port capacity give external operators disproportionate leverage over mining and agricultural exports. Chinese, Gulf, European, and regional actors are competing for influence over logistics and strategic commodities.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens a narrow recovery window

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains heavily dependent on IMF-backed reforms, donor support, and debt restructuring, limiting policy autonomy over public investment and foreign-exchange management.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare earths, and niobium projects are attracting foreign capital, but weak infrastructure and regulatory capacity could leave the state with limited value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenues, raising litigation, production, and investment risks in the gold sector.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security footprint
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has displaced Western influence but has not resolved insurgency, while increasing sovereignty risks around strategic mining and political decision-making.

highlights: Offshore gas enters the strategic equation
Iron and green-hydrogen plans seek leverage

frictionVectors.title: Gas-project dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export potential, but foreign operators, shared infrastructure, and contractual dependence constrain Mauritania's control over downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and hydrogen infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, iron-ore, and green-hydrogen projects could diversify the economy, yet financing terms and land-use pressures remain significant sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos implementation risk
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has advanced diplomatically, but the future of the Diego Garcia base and the terms of any long-term lease remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External trade and energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: The island's dependence on imported fuel, foreign shipping routes, and external markets leaves infrastructure and food-energy security vulnerable to geopolitical shocks.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables reinforce strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara contestation
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and resource development in Western Sahara remain contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front, creating persistent diplomatic and legal exposure for infrastructure investors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. investment supports ports, renewables, fertilizers, and logistics, but also creates leverage over critical infrastructure and export chains.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gas projects remain exposed to insurgency and depend on foreign security support, constraining Maputo's control over strategic energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG infrastructure and contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: International operators and lenders dominate financing and technical capacity, limiting domestic value capture despite large gas reserves.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen reshape strategy

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent discoveries could strengthen state revenues, but foreign-led exploration and limited domestic capacity create risks of enclave development.

frictionVectors.title: Green hydrogen financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale hydrogen projects rely heavily on European and other external capital, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnership realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's break with French and Western security partners has increased reliance on Russia-linked support while insurgent violence continues to threaten transport and mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and refinery exposure
frictionVectors.details: New oil-export infrastructure offers greater fiscal autonomy but remains vulnerable to political disputes, border insecurity, and dependence on external operators.

frictionVectors.title: IOC divestment and asset control
frictionVectors.details: International firms are reshaping upstream holdings, while regulatory uncertainty and financing constraints complicate Nigeria's effort to retain value in the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline theft and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, and conflict in producing regions continue to reduce public revenues and weaken effective control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: International allegations concerning mineral flows linked to the eastern DRC conflict create persistent diplomatic and reputational pressure on Kigali.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong policy autonomy, but dependence on external donors, investors, and regional trade corridors limits complete control over infrastructure and resource value chains.

highlights: Offshore Oil Hopes, Limited Bargaining Power
Maritime Security Anchored in External Partnerships

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe retains formal control over prospective offshore blocks but lacks the capital and technical capacity to develop them independently. Oil expectations risk increasing leverage for foreign operators before commercially viable reserves are confirmed.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on external partners for maritime surveillance, port modernization, and economic infrastructure. This creates strategic exposure around the Gulf of Guinea without indicating a single dominant foreign patron.

highlights: Resource Sovereignty Agenda Meets Production Reality
Gas and Oil Revenue Framework Under Scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN OPERATOR RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national participation and improved fiscal terms in oil and gas projects, but relies heavily on international firms for financing, technology, and operations. Contract revisions could strain investor confidence and public finances.

frictionVectors.title: SENEGALESE-MAURITANIAN GAS COORDINATION
frictionVectors.details: The shared GTA gas project requires sustained coordination over revenue distribution, security, and local-content expectations. Delays or disputes could weaken Dakar's ability to convert offshore production into broad domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from tuna access agreements and foreign investment but faces persistent concerns over transparency, stock depletion, and whether licensing revenues adequately benefit the domestic economy. Its limited enforcement capacity constrains effective control of surrounding waters.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Maritime surveillance, port facilities, and coast-guard capabilities depend on partnerships with larger powers, including India and other international actors. Victoria generally balances these relationships to avoid surrendering strategic autonomy.

highlights: Mining Revenue Versus Domestic Value Capture

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and operators, while local processing and fiscal capture remain limited. Commodity-price volatility and concession disputes can quickly affect public revenue and political stability.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked port and transport infrastructure gives external investors significant influence over export corridors. The government must balance urgently needed investment against concerns about long-term control of strategic logistics assets.

highlights: Resource Sovereignty Constrained by Fragmented Authority

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL LICENSING DISPUTES
frictionVectors.details: Federal and regional authorities continue to face tension over ownership, licensing, and revenue sharing for offshore hydrocarbons. Foreign companies and partner governments can exploit institutional fragmentation when contracts are not nationally coordinated.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, SECURITY, AND EXTERNAL PATRONS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners provide security, port, and infrastructure support while seeking strategic and commercial access. Al-Shabaab insurgency and weak federal control make it difficult for Somalia to impose consistent sovereign regulation across its territory and waters.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and grid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent Eskom reliability problems constrain industrial sovereignty and encourage reliance on private generation, imported equipment, and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral beneficiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth inputs while balancing investment needs from China, the United States, and European partners.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan export-route disruption
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on infrastructure crossing Sudan to move crude to Port Sudan, leaving public revenue and energy exports exposed to the Sudanese conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled oil economy
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-linked operators retain major leverage over production, services, and financing, while weak institutions limit domestic control over oil rents.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-smuggling networks
frictionVectors.details: Conflict actors and cross-border intermediaries compete for gold flows, reducing state revenue and increasing leverage for external patrons and regional trading hubs.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Fighting threatens Port Sudan, oil infrastructure, and humanitarian supply corridors, leaving remaining export capacity vulnerable to military control and foreign security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening local-content, fiscal, and processing requirements for gold and critical minerals, creating friction with multinational operators over licensing and profit distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam port and regional rail corridors strengthens Tanzania's leverage, but major projects remain dependent on foreign contractors, lenders, and technology providers.

frictionVectors.title: Port-led external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a transshipment and regional trade hub brings revenue and strategic influence but also exposes national infrastructure policy to foreign shipping, finance, and security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector modernization
frictionVectors.details: The state retains a central role in phosphate development while relying on external capital and expertise, creating recurring tension between production expansion and domestic value capture.

highlights: Phosphate and energy sovereignty under strain

frictionVectors.title: EU Financing and Migration Bargain
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain closely tied to migration control, giving Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal pressure limits Tunis's ability to resist externally shaped priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to price shocks and foreign financing conditions. Declining phosphate output further weakens a traditionally important source of sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Transit Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's export strategy but faces financing, environmental, and political pressure from Western institutions and civil society. Delays could increase Uganda's dependence on external investors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major role in roads, hydropower, and energy construction, expanding infrastructure capacity while increasing repayment and procurement dependence. Kampala is balancing Beijing against Gulf, Indian, and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing, tax capture, and strategic control over copper expansion, but foreign mining capital still dominates technology, financing, and market access. Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors gives Lusaka leverage but also creates dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral support have stabilized Zambia's external position but limit fiscal flexibility. Transport corridors, power supply, and mining investment remain vulnerable to creditor and investor conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms dominate much of Zimbabwe's lithium processing and mining expansion, while Western and regional investors compete for platinum, gold, and other critical minerals. Export restrictions have improved stated beneficiation goals but enforcement and local value capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Finance, and Strategic Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions and restricted access to international finance push Harare toward China, Russia, and opaque bilateral arrangements. The resulting bargaining space preserves regime autonomy but often weakens transparency and Zimbabwe's ability to secure favorable resource terms.
